name: Kiembu
confidence_why: Every source that speaks to Kiembu prosody calls it a tone language with high and low tones — Mwaniki 2014, Mutahi 1977 and Nyaga 2014 from their own Kiembu data, Gatumu 2014 for the Mbeere variety, and Philippson 1991 for the Central Kenya (Thagicu) group as a whole — and Philippson's hedged, group-level suggestion of a non-contrastive penultimate accent riding on the tones does not dispute that…

catalog_quote: Hyman (1975) refers to stress, tone and duration as suprasegmentals of prominence. He states that these features are always present in all utterances and hence any utterance in any language is characterized by differing degrees of loudness, melody and rhythm. The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone. Tone plays a very significant role in bringing out a number of contrasts such as in lexical differentiation, in tense and aspect constructs. [p. 30] ... Mutahi (1977), states that Kiembu is a tonal language. He adds that, tone plays an important role in dialect classification. He also notes that a word that begins in a low tone (L) in one dialect may begin with a high tone (H) in another dialect and may have a sequence of two high tones in a third dialect. [p. 31] ... Kiembu has high (H) and low (L) tone. The tones are represented in lexical items across Kiembu lexicon on syllabic…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Embu (embu1241) is not in the catalog. Two title-hit items: (1) Philippson 1991 (open PDF from DDL/CNRS, already downloaded by the gwen1239 check; copied into and read) — Embu is a '+' sample language with the author's own field notes, but the thesis has no Embu-specific prosodic statement or Annexe entry; the group-level claim (p. 451, p. 460, p. 485) is that Thagicu languages other than Kikuyu, 'semble-t-il', share the Kamba system: four Common-Bantu tone schemes plus a lexical opposition between (default) penultimate accent and exceptional final accent, the penultimate accent being demarcative and realised (in Kamba) as L-tone register, not length. (2) Torres Cacoullos & Travis 2014 is about English; Glottolog attached it to Embu by a computerized keyword misassignment ('patterning') — irrelevant. Best Embu-specific first-hand sources held by the project (earlier check, re-checked) are Mwaniki 2014 pp. 30/33 ('tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu') and Nyaga 2014 p. 72 (emphatic penultimate lengthening); no source read gives a firm word-stress position for Embu. Lead for acquisition: Möhlig 1974 (Die Stellung der Bergdialekte im Osten des Mt. Kenya), Philippson's only Embu/Meru source, print-only (not an item here). direct download, Crossref and Glottolog worked. updated.

He states that these features are always present in all utterances.. The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone. Tone plays a very significant role in bringing out a number of contrasts such as in lexical differentiation, in tense and aspect constructs.' (p. 30); 'Mutahi (1977), states that Kiembu is a tonal langua…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kiembu is a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone; the source names stress among the possible suprasegmentals and then states that tone is the only suprasegmental feature of Kiembu, i.e. no word stress is recognised. No stress position is given anywhere in the opened sources. A weaker secondary hint (Nyaga 2014: 72) is that vowels are lengthened in the penultimate syllable in emphatic speech, but that claim is borrowed from a Gikuyu thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone section notes dialect differences in tone patterns (LH in Embu North/West vs LHLH in Embu East, sec. 3.2.4, pp. 39-40) but nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical items in citation form, nouns and verbs); tone is discussed 'on syllabic basis'. Nyaga's penultimate lengthening remark concerns emphatic/reduplicated forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Mwaniki 2014 describes Kiembu proper (dialect areas Embu North/West vs Embu East, Kiruguru mentioned); Mbeere/Kimbeere (treated as a dialect of Embu in Wikipedia and in Mutahi 1977; Gatumu 2014 and Njuki 2012 are Kimbeere-specific) is not the variety of the quoted statement. Mutahi 1977 covers the whole Southern Mt. Kenya dialect continuum (Kikuyu, Embu, Mbeere). Glottolog's descriptive reference list for embu1241 is mostly keyword noise ('patterning'); only Biersteker 1984 and Saberwal 1968 actually concern Embu.

new_statements.quote: Cette apparition est due, d'une part, à la création de tons modulés lexicaux (selon des modalités que nous allons examiner) et, en kamba comme, semble-t-il, dans le reste des parlers du groupe, à une opposition entre accent sur la pénultième et accent sur la finale (se reporter au Chapitre cinq, 3.12.1). Je n'ai pas d'explication à proposer sur l'origine de cette opposition, autre que l'emprunt des thèmes accentués sur la finale.
new_statements.translation: This appearance [of new tone schemes] is due, on the one hand, to the creation of lexical contour tones (in ways we shall examine) and, in Kamba as, it seems, in the rest of the dialects of the group, to an opposition between accent on the penultimate and accent on the final syllable (see Chapter five, 3.12.1). I have no explanation to offer for the origin of this opposition other than the borrowing of finally-accented stems.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris V. (Glottolog 38907)
new_statements.locator: p. 451 (ch. 6 §2.8.1, group XXII Thagicu); supporting p. 460 (typology a') and p. 485 (§3.5.3)
new_statements.reading: Group-level, not Embu-specific: Embu (E52) is a Thagicu language for which Philippson (who had his own Embu notes, p. 515) infers, hedged with 'semble-t-il', the Kamba pattern — a tonal language with a demarcative penultimate accent (realised in Kamba as register of L tones, pp. 368-369) contrasting with exceptional final accent on a minority of (mostly borrowed) stems; Kikuyu is explicitly excluded from this (p. 460, p. 485). The only first-hand Embu-specific statements held by the project remain Mwaniki 2014 pp. 30 and 33 ('The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone' / 'tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu'), which deny stress rather than locate it, and Nyaga 2014 p. 72 (penultimate vowel lengthening in emphatic speech, citing a Gikuyu thesis). Not a firm statement of word-stress position for Embu.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

new_statements.quote: Tous les autres parlers du groupe (à l'exception, peut-être, du sonjo, très divergent et très mal attesté) ont conservé cette quadruple répartition. Mais, par ailleurs, de nouveaux schèmes sont apparus dans la plupart des langues.: 5 en kikuyu, 4 en kamba, etc. Cette apparition est due, d'une part, à la création de tons modulés lexicaux (selon des modalités que nous allons examiner) et, en kamba comme, semble-t-il, dans le reste des parlers du groupe, à une opposition entre accent sur la pénultième et accent sur la finale (se reporter au Chapitre cinq, 3.12.1). Je n'ai pas d'explication à proposer sur l'origine de cette opposition, autre que l'emprunt des thèmes accentués sur la finale. [pp. 450-451]
new_statements.translation: All the other varieties of the group (except, perhaps, Sonjo, very divergent and very poorly attested) have kept this fourfold [Common Bantu tone] distribution. But, in addition, new patterns have appeared in most of the languages: 5 in Kikuyu, 4 in Kamba, etc. This appearance is due, on the one hand, to the creation of lexical contour tones (in ways we shall examine) and, in Kamba as, it seems, in the rest of the varieties of the group, to an opposition between accent on the penultimate and accent on the final (see Chapter five, 3.12.1). I have no explanation to offer for the origin of this opposition, other than borrowing of the finally-accented stems.

new_statements.relation_note: Same work and same p. 451 passage as the second existing_statement (Philippson 1991); re-read confirms that statement exactly, including its hedged, group-level character and the absence of any Embu-specific data. Compatible with Mwaniki 2014 ('tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu') because Philippson's accent is a demarcative (non-contrastive) penultimate prominence realised through tonal register, not a stress contrast. Adds p. 485: 'l'interaction entre l'accent (pénultième ou exceptionnellement final) et le système tonal, qui crée de nouvelles catégories prosodiques en chaga et dans les langues du groupe du Kenya Central', and the annexe entry for Kamba p. 513: 'langue tonale,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tonal languages of the Thagicu group (Embu is listed in the sample, p. 73, with the author's own field notes, p. 515) are said, at group level and with the hedge 'semble-t-il', to have a demarcative accent on the penultimate syllable, opposed to an exceptional final accent on a minority of (mostly borrowed) stems; in Kamba, the only group member for which the mechanism is worked out (p. 368), this accent is realised not as length but as pitch register of low tones (an accented L is higher than a post-accent L). Kikuyu is explicitly excluded (p. 460 typology a'; p. 485 class e 'la pénultième ne semble jouer aucun rôle'). No Embu-specific data or statement anywhere in the thesis (no Embu entry in the annexe, pp. 513-514; bibliography for 'EMBU, MERU' is only Möhlig 1974, p. 527).
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent on a minority of stems, attributed to borrowing (p. 451, and footnote 1 p. 451: imperatives seem to be finally accented, possibly an intonation effect); in Kamba, monosyllables show no accent contrast and stems ending in H show no accentual variation (p. 369). Kikuyu excluded from the penultimate-accent pattern (pp. 460, 485).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's statements are about the Thagicu / Kenya Central group (XXII) as a whole, with Kamba (E.55) as the worked example and Kikuyu (E.51) explicitly excluded; Embu (E.52) is in his sample (p. 73, single '+', own field notes p. 515) but receives no separate description, no annexe entry, and only Möhlig 1974 in the bibliography (p. 527). Nothing opened describes a particular Embu dialect.

new_statements.quote: En revanche, on peut considérer comme fondamentaux : - l'interaction entre l'accent (pénultième ou exceptionnellement final) et le système tonal, qui crée de nouvelles catégories prosodiques en chaga et dans les langues du groupe du Kenya Central. Cette évolution est unique en Afrique Orientale et le fait qu'elle se rencontre dans deux groupes contigus laisse envisager une influence de type "aréal". [p. 485] [...] admettons que les mots kamba soient normalement affectés d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième, comme c'est le cas de nombreuses langues bantu à l'est de la Rift Valley (cf. le chapitre suivant). Cet accent ne peut se réaliser comme une longueur [...] et se réalise donc comme une modification du niveau des B. [p. 368]
new_statements.translation: On the other hand, one may regard as fundamental: - the interaction between the accent (penultimate or exceptionally final) and the tone system, which creates new prosodic categories in Chaga and in the languages of the Central Kenya group. This development is unique in East Africa and the fact that it occurs in two contiguous groups suggests an 'areal' influence. [p. 485] [...] let us assume that Kamba words normally bear a demarcative accent on the penultimate, as is the case in many Bantu languages east of the Rift Valley (cf. the next chapter). This accent cannot be realised as length [...] and is therefore realised as a modification of the level of the L tones. [p. 368]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Same thesis as work 0 (the READALL list carries it twice under 1991 and 1992). Group-level claim for the Central Kenya (Thagicu) languages: tonal systems with a demarcative penultimate accent, exceptionally final on some stems, interacting with the four inherited Common Bantu tone patterns; Kamba is the worked example (accent realised as tonal register, p. 368; annexe p. 513 'langue tonale, avec accent lexical partiellement libre'). Embu itself receives no separate statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Exceptional final accent (borrowed stems; imperatives); Kikuyu excluded (p. 485 class e).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's statements are about the Thagicu / Kenya Central group (XXII) as a whole, with Kamba (E.55) as the worked example and Kikuyu (E.51) explicitly excluded; Embu (E.52) is in his sample (p. 73, single '+', own field notes p. 515) but receives no separate description, no annexe entry, and only Möhlig 1974 in the bibliography (p. 527). Nothing opened describes a particular Embu dialect.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between sources. Philippson 1991/1992 (pp. 450-451, 485) posits, at group level and hedged with 'semble-t-il', a demarcative penultimate accent (exceptionally final on borrowed stems) for the Thagicu languages other than Kikuyu, worked out only for Kamba (p. 368, realised as tonal register); Mwaniki 2014 (already held by the project, pp. 30, 33) says tone is the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu. These are compatible: Philippson's accent is a non-contrastive demarcative prominence expressed through tone, not a stress contrast, and Philippson gives no Embu-specific data at all. Nevins & Chitoran 2008 is silent (abstract only; body not obtainable). No source locates word stress in Embu itself.
